column1: In SQL Server, a CTE definition must be followed by the {{c1::single statement}} that uses it.
column2: A CTE is scoped to the next statement. Other statements cannot refer to it.

column1: In a recursive CTE, the {{c1::anchor member}} provides the initial result set.
column2: The recursive member builds on previous results.

column1: In SQL Server, OPTION (MAXRECURSION {{c1::0}}) removes the recursion limit for a recursive CTE.
column2: Use a termination condition even when the limit is removed. An unbounded recursion can consume resources.

column1: The {{c1::PARTITION BY}} clause divides rows into groups for a window calculation without reducing the row count.
column2: A window function returns a value for each input row.

column1: For tied values, {{c1::DENSE_RANK}} does not leave gaps in the sequence of ranks.
column2: RANK leaves gaps after ties. ROW_NUMBER assigns a different number to each row.

column1: In SQL Server, LAG(value) reads a value from a {{c1::preceding}} row in the ordered partition.
column2: Use LEAD to read a following row. The window ORDER BY defines the sequence.

column1: A SQL Server ROWS window frame counts {{c1::physical rows}} in the ordered partition.
column2: For repeatable row-by-row results when order values tie, include a unique tie-breaker.

column1: To calculate a partition-wide LAST_VALUE, the frame must extend through {{c1::UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING}}.
column2: For example, use ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING.

column1: In SQL Server, JSON_QUERY extracts a JSON {{c1::object or array}} from a document.
column2: JSON_VALUE extracts a scalar value instead.

column1: In a SQL Server JSON path, {{c1::strict}} mode raises an error when the requested path is missing.
column2: Lax mode is the default and returns NULL for a missing path.

column1: SQL Server OPENJSON requires database compatibility level {{c1::130}} or higher.
column2: OPENJSON converts JSON to a rowset. Check the target database compatibility level.

column1: An OPENJSON {{c1::WITH}} clause defines an explicit output schema with SQL types and JSON paths.
column2: Use it to map JSON properties to named and typed columns.

column1: SQL Server JSON_MODIFY returns JSON text with a {{c1::modified value}} at a specified path.
column2: Assign or use the returned text. The function does not independently persist the change to a table.

column1: A SQL Server indexed computed column can expose a JSON property extracted with {{c1::JSON_VALUE}}.
column2: Match the query expression to the computed expression and choose an appropriate data type.

column1: In SQL Server 2025, REGEXP_LIKE requires database compatibility level {{c1::170}} or higher.
column2: REGEXP_LIKE is a predicate. Other regex functions have different compatibility requirements.

column1: In a regular expression, the {{c1::^}} anchor matches the start of the input.
column2: For example, ^AB matches AB at the beginning of a string.

column1: In SQL Server 2025, REGEXP_SPLIT_TO_TABLE returns {{c1::rows}} split by a regular expression pattern.
column2: It is a table-valued function. Check availability on the target platform.

column1: In SQL Server 2025, a smaller EDIT_DISTANCE value means the strings require {{c1::fewer edits}} to match.
column2: The function is in preview. An exact match has an edit distance of zero.

column1: In SQL Server 2025, JARO_WINKLER_SIMILARITY uses an integer scale from 0 to {{c1::100}}.
column2: A score of 100 indicates a full match. The function is in preview in SQL Server 2025.

column1: In a SQL Server graph, an {{c1::edge}} table stores directed relationships between nodes.
column2: For example, a Follows edge can connect one Person node to another.

column1: In SQL Server graph queries, the {{c1::MATCH}} predicate specifies a relationship pattern.
column2: The pattern uses node and edge aliases declared in the FROM clause.

column1: An EXISTS subquery is true when it returns {{c1::at least one row}}.
column2: EXISTS tests row existence. The selected values do not determine the result.

column1: A correlated subquery references a column from the {{c1::outer query}}.
column2: The optimizer can transform the query, so the logical correlation does not guarantee a literal per-row execution strategy.

column1: In SQL Server, XACT_STATE() returns {{c1::-1}} when the transaction is uncommittable.
column2: An uncommittable transaction must be rolled back rather than committed.

column1: In a SQL Server CATCH block, {{c1::ERROR_NUMBER()}} returns the number of the error being handled.
column2: Other error functions provide details such as message, severity, and line number.
